question: How does pasteurization make milk safe to drink?

passages.title: How Does Pasteurization Change Milk and Other Beverages?
passages.text: Pasteurization makes milk and many other beverages safer to drink by using controlled heat to destroy disease-causing microorganisms and reduce the number of organisms that cause spoilage. The process can also change a beverage’s flavor, aroma, texture, and nutritional properties, although the effects depend on the temperature, heating time, composition of the drink, and how it is packaged and stored afterward. In milk, pasteurization is designed to eliminate harmful bacteria without producing the pronounced cooked flavor associated with more intensive heat treatments. It does not make milk completely sterile, and it does not prevent all spoilage. Instead, it reduces microbial risks and extends the time milk remains suitable for consumption when handled and refrigerated properly. The same principle applies to many other beverages, including fruit juices, cider, beer, and certain plant-based drinks. However, each beverage presents different challenges because its acidity, sugar content, proteins, and other ingredients influence how microorganisms respond to heat. What pasteurization does to microorganisms Pasteurization is a controlled heat treatment that reduces harmful microorganisms to a level considered safe for a particular food or beverage. It was developed through the work of French scientist Louis Pasteur, whose research helped establish that microorganisms are responsible for fermentation

From the cow to your cup, the U.S. dairy industry follows many strict government regulations, including milk pasteurization, to ensure that milk is safe to drink. When it comes to ensuring the safety of milk and other dairy foods, University of Wisconsin-Madison food science professor John Lucey says pasteurization is the best line of defense. “Pasteurization is an absolutely critical control point for making dairy products safe,” Lucey said. “There really isn’t another single aspect that is as important as it is. If there is a pathogen or anything in the milk that we don’t want, pasteurization destroys it. It is our industry’s shield.” Over the past decades and centuries, as farmers learned to make more food with fewer resources, most of us have shifted from living on farms or in rural settings to cities. Recent reports that the H5N1 avian flu virus has been found in cow’s milk have raised questions about whether the U.S. milk supply is safe to drink. According to the federal Food and Drug Administration, the answer is yes, as long as the milk is pasteurized. Nonetheless, raw (unpasteurized) milk sales are up, despite health experts’ warning that raw milk could contain high levels of the virus, along with many other pathogens. Pasteurization does not necessarily destroy bacterial spores, dormant structures that allow certain bacteria to survive harsh conditions. These spores can later develop into active bacteria under favorable conditions. For this reason, ordinary pasteurization cannot be treated as a guarantee that a beverage is sterile or safe under every storage condition. How milk is pasteurized Milk provides an especially clear example of how pasteurization balances safety with quality. Raw milk can contain disease-causing microorganisms introduced by an infected animal, contaminated equipment, the surrounding environment, or handling during collection and processing. Proper sanitation reduces these risks, but it cannot eliminate them reliably on its own. Several heat-treatment methods are used to make milk safer. The two familiar approaches are high-temperature, short-time pasteurization and low-temperature, long-time pasteurization. High-temperature, short-time pasteurization, commonly called HTST, typically heats milk to at least 161°F (72°C) for 15 seconds. Low-temperature, long-time pasteurization, or LTLT, typically heats milk to at least 145°F (63°C) for 30 minutes. Avian flu in milk The detection of avian flu virus fragments in milk is a new challenge for the dairy industry. Scientists do not have a full picture of the risks to humans but are learning. Research so far has shown that virus particles end up in the milk of infected cows, but that pasteurization will inactivate the virus. However, the FDA is advising consumers not to drink raw milk because there is limited information about whether it may transmit avian flu. The agency also is urging producers not to manufacture or sell raw milk or raw milk products, including cheese, made with milk from cows showing symptoms of illness. It’s never a good time to get a foodborne illness, and this is the beginning of ice cream season. At a time when avian flu is showing up in new species and scientists are still learning about how it is transmitted, I agree with the FDA that raw milk poses risks not worth taking. passages.text: Terms like “milk pasteurization” may be unfamiliar to some, and even a few who question what pasteurization means. The milk pasteurization process is one of the many strict government regulations that the U.S. dairy industry must meet to ensure milk safety. But how did we get there and what does pasteurization mean? Find out below. What is pasteurization? Milk pasteurization is the process of heating milk to a specific temperature for a set period of time in order to kill harmful bacteria that can be found in raw milk. The goal of pasteurization is not to boil or sterilize milk. It’s simply to lower the risk of harmful microorganisms while keeping milk usable, nutritious, and fresh-tasting. When was pasteurization invented? About 160 years ago, Louis Pasteur developed the pasteurization process while he was tasked with finding practical solutions for problems such as keeping harmful bacteria at bay in different foods. The dairy industry’s commitment to assuring safe products has a long history that dates to 1924 with the creation of the Standard Milk Ordinance developed by the U.S. Public Health Service. Its proteins, fats, lactose, and minerals remain largely intact, so pasteurized milk continues to provide protein, calcium, phosphorus, and other nutrients found in raw milk. Milk proteins can change their structure during heating without losing all their nutritional value. Some whey proteins, which remain dissolved in the liquid portion of milk, unfold when heated. This process is called denaturation. It changes the proteins’ physical structure and behavior, but it does not automatically make them nutritionally useless. Casein, the main family of proteins responsible for much of milk’s structure, is comparatively resistant to ordinary pasteurization conditions. Calcium and phosphorus are minerals, so pasteurization does not destroy them in the way heat can degrade certain vitamins. Heating can influence how some minerals are distributed between dissolved and protein-associated forms, but it does not substantially eliminate milk’s overall mineral content. Some vitamins are more sensitive to heat than others. Vitamin C and certain B vitamins can be affected by processing, although the amount lost during ordinary milk pasteurization is generally limited. Because milk is not a major source of vitamin C, this change usually has little effect on its overall nutritional role. More intensive treatments can cause greater losses of some

These are established time-and-temperature combinations for milk, and commercial processing must meet applicable requirements for the product and equipment. In HTST processing, milk flows through a heat exchanger, where it is rapidly warmed, held at the required temperature for the prescribed time, and then cooled. The system is designed to ensure that the milk receives the necessary treatment. If the required conditions are not met, properly designed equipment can divert the milk away from the finished-product stream for further processing. Rapid heating and cooling help limit unnecessary exposure to heat. As a result, pasteurized milk retains much of the taste and nutritional character of fresh milk while becoming substantially safer to drink. Pasteurization is not the same as boiling. Boiling generally exposes milk to a higher temperature for longer than standard pasteurization, which can produce more noticeable changes in flavor and the behavior of milk proteins. Properly pasteurized milk does not need to be boiled again for safety under normal handling conditions. Milk’s nutritional value also depends on factors unrelated to pasteurization, including whether it is whole or reduced-fat, whether it has been fortified, and whether other ingredients have been added. For example, vitamin D in many U.S. milk products is present because it is added during processing, not because pasteurization creates it. Pasteurization does not make milk nutritionally empty, nor does it eliminate its main benefits as a source of protein and minerals. How pasteurization changes milk’s taste, smell, and texture Most people notice relatively little difference between raw milk and conventionally pasteurized milk when the products are otherwise comparable. Nevertheless, heating can produce subtle sensory changes. Milk’s natural flavor comes from a mixture of compounds associated with its fat, proteins, sugars, and other constituents. Heat can alter some of these compounds and create new ones. Depending on the treatment, milk may develop a slightly cooked aroma or taste. Processing decisions therefore involve several connected goals: controlling harmful microorganisms, reducing spoilage, preserving taste and texture, retaining nutrients, and achieving the desired storage life. More intensive heat treatment can provide greater microbial stability, but it may also produce more noticeable changes in flavor or other qualities. The central idea is that pasteurization is not simply a way to heat a beverage. It is a controlled process designed to make a product safer and more stable while limiting unwanted changes. When combined with appropriate sanitation, packaging, and storage, it helps milk and many other beverages remain safe and retain the qualities that make them useful and enjoyable.

The appropriate heat treatment must account for both microbial safety and the drink’s physical stability. Nutritional changes also depend on the ingredients and process. Fortification adds another variable because the behavior of added vitamins and minerals depends on their chemical form and the conditions under which they are processed. Consequently, there is no single description of how pasteurization changes every plant-based beverage. A thin almond drink, a protein-rich soy beverage, and a starch-containing oat beverage may respond differently to the same general category of heat treatment. Why pasteurization does not eliminate every food safety risk Pasteurization is a major food safety measure, but it is only one part of a larger system. Its effectiveness depends on the product receiving the required treatment throughout the process and remaining protected from contamination afterward. A beverage can become contaminated after pasteurization if it comes into contact with unclean equipment, contaminated surfaces, or improperly handled packaging. What can make milk unsafe Dairy products, like many foods, have inherent risks that can cause a variety of illnesses and even death. Our milk comes from animals that graze outdoors and live in barns. Milk is picked up from the farm in tanker trucks and delivered to the processing plant. These environments offer numerous opportunities for contamination by pathogens that cause illness and organisms that make food spoil. For example, listeria monocytogenes comes from environmental sources like soil and water. Mild infections with listeriosis cause flu-like symptoms. More serious cases are, unfortunately, too common and can cause miscarriages in pregnant women and even death in extreme cases. Other pathogens commonly associated with dairy animals and raw milk include E. coli, which can cause severe gastrointestinal infections and may lead to kidney damage; Campylobacter, the most common cause of diarrheal illness in the U.S.; and Salmonella, which cause abdominal pain, diarrhea and other symptoms. Milk’s shelf life therefore depends on several interacting factors: the effectiveness of the heat treatment, cleanliness during processing and packaging, storage temperature, packaging integrity, and the characteristics of the product itself. A carton of pasteurized milk can still spoil before its printed date if it is left warm for too long or contaminated after opening. Conversely, properly refrigerated milk may remain acceptable for a period that depends on its processing and storage history. The printed date is not a substitute for safe handling, and milk showing signs of spoilage should not be consumed. How ultra-high-temperature processing differs from pasteurization Some milk undergoes ultra-high-temperature processing, commonly called UHT. This method exposes milk to a much higher temperature, typically around 275°F (135°C) or above, for a few seconds. The milk is then placed in sterile packaging under conditions designed to prevent recontamination. UHT processing destroys far more microorganisms, including many organisms and spores that can survive ordinary pasteurization. When combined with appropriate aseptic packaging, it produces commercially sterile milk that can remain shelf-stable while unopened. How plant-based beverages respond to pasteurization Soy, oat, almond, and other plant-based beverages are often heat-treated to reduce microbial risks and improve shelf life. Although they may resemble milk in appearance and use, their chemical composition differs considerably from dairy milk. Plant-based beverages can contain varying amounts of protein, starch, fat, sugar, fiber, and suspended particles. These components influence how the beverage responds to heating. For example, starch in oat beverages can change its behavior when heated, affecting thickness and texture. Plant proteins can also unfold, aggregate, or interact with other ingredients. Heating may alter the stability of an emulsion, a mixture in which droplets of one liquid are dispersed in another. In beverages containing plant oils, changes in the interactions among oil droplets, proteins, and stabilizing ingredients can affect whether the product remains uniform or separates during storage. Why pasteurized milk lasts longer Milk naturally contains nutrients that support microbial growth, including water, proteins, sugars, fats, and minerals. These make it valuable as food for people, but they can also provide favorable conditions for microorganisms. Raw milk may contain bacteria that multiply during storage, even when it is refrigerated. As they grow, some microorganisms break down milk components, producing acids and other substances that cause sourness, off-flavors, odors, or curdling. Pasteurization reduces the initial population of microorganisms, including many that contribute to spoilage. With fewer surviving organisms, deterioration generally takes longer, especially when milk is kept cold. Refrigeration remains essential because pasteurization does not remove every microorganism. Some heat-resistant organisms may survive, and contamination can occur after treatment through equipment, containers, or handling. Certain surviving bacteria can also grow at refrigerator temperatures, although usually more slowly than they would at warmer temperatures. Milk’s shelf life therefore depends on several interacting factors: the effectiveness of the heat treatment, cleanliness during processing and packaging, storage temperature, packaging integrity, and the characteristics of the product itself. Heating can also change the behavior of proteins. Denatured whey proteins may interact with other milk components, affecting how the milk responds to later processing. These effects are particularly important in products such as yogurt, cheese, and other dairy foods, where protein structure influences texture and manufacturing performance. Ordinary pasteurization does not substantially change the basic composition of milk or cause its fat to disappear. Separation of cream is instead influenced by whether the milk has been homogenized. Homogenization is a separate mechanical process that breaks fat globules into smaller droplets, helping prevent cream from rising to the surface. Pasteurization and homogenization are often performed as parts of the same commercial production process, but they serve different purposes. Pasteurization controls microorganisms; homogenization changes the physical distribution of fat. Pasteurization compared with raw beverages Raw milk and some unpasteurized juices may retain certain microorganisms and enzymes that would be reduced or inactivated by heat treatment. However, the presence of living microorganisms does not automatically make a beverage healthier, and the absence of pasteurization does not guarantee that beneficial organisms will be present. Raw milk can carry pathogens such as Salmonella, Campylobacter, pathogenic Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes. These organisms can cause serious illness, and contamination may occur even when the milk appears clean and smells normal. Children, older adults, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems are particularly vulnerable to severe outcomes from certain foodborne infections. Unpasteurized juice can also contain harmful microorganisms. Its acidity reduces the growth of many bacteria but does not reliably eliminate pathogens that may have entered through contaminated fruit, equipment, or handling.
